study.title: Psalm 47 God reigns over all nations
study.overview: This psalm summons all peoples to praise the LORD because he reigns as a sovereign king over the whole earth. The poem begins with a universal call to joy and reverence, passes to God's saving actions in behalf of his people and culminates in the vision of rulers and nations gathered under the rule of Abraham's God. The emphasis is not only on Israel, but on the universal government of God and the inclusion of nations in their kingdom.

outline.title: Universal Call to Praise
outline.explanation: All peoples are called to clap and cry out with joy, because the Most High Lord is fearful and reigns over the whole earth. Praise is born of the recognition of majesty and divine sovereignty.

outline.title: The victories of God and His exaltation
outline.explanation: The psalm recalls that God subjectes the peoples, chooses the inheritance of his people and rises with acclaim, a celebrative language that highlights his victory and his reign. Therefore, the people are repeatedly exhorted to sing praises to their King.

outline.title: God reigns over everyone and gathers the nations
outline.explanation: Worship must be intelligent and conscious, because God reigns over the nations and is enthroned in holiness. The end extends the vision: heads of the peoples join the people of the God of Abraham, showing that divine dominion reaches the peoples of the whole earth.

study.context: The notes note that the psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah and was used to celebrate God's reign over all the earth. Some interpreters mentioned in the notes relate him to God's victory in favor of Israel and also to a broader reading, in which Jews and nations participate in the divine kingdom. There is also a reading that connects it to events linked to the restoration of Israel and, in a spiritual sense, to the inclusion of nations in the people of God. These readings appear as interpretations, not as mandatory statements of the text.
study.theology: The psalm teaches God's universal sovereignty: he is not only the God of a people, but King of the whole earth. His majesty demands public praise, joyful and conscious. At the same time, her royalty is not abstract; it manifests itself in concrete acts of salvation, in the choice of the inheritance of its people and in the gathering of peoples and rulers under its lordship. The final phrase points to the supreme exaltation of God, which governs even those who seemed stronger, called here of shields from the earth. Theologically, psalm unites adoration and dominion: to praise God is to recognize who he is and what he does. It also suggests that the divine plan reaches the nations, and not only Israel, although the notes present this as a prophetic or spiritual reading.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm celebrates the royalty of God over all the earth and shows that Israel and the nations share in their kingdom.
The goal of the psalm is to encourage all to praise God in a public, joyful and understanding way.
The verse presents the meeting of the peoples under God, read in the notes such as the union of Jews and Gentiles in their people.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that God reigns over the whole earth, and not just about our particular life?
How can our words and songs be more conscious and understood rather than merely repeated?
How does the vision of peoples gathered to God's people correct any spiritual pride or exclusivism?
study.practice: Practice a praise that is public, cheerful and conscious. Separate a moment to thank God for a concrete act of care and then pray recognizing his sovereignty over his family, church, city and nations. If you participate in congregational worship, be careful about the content of the words, not just the melody. And if there are barriers between you and other people, remember that the God of Abraham gathers people under your lordship; this must produce humility, hospitality, and desire to witness.
study.uncertainty: The notes offer different historical and spiritual readings: some associate the psalm with the restoration of Israel, others to the ascension of Christ and the inclusion of the Gentiles. The text itself clearly affirms the universal sovereignty of God and the gathering of nations, but it does not specify all the details of these applications alone. There is also ambiguity in the final expression about the peoples and on the shields of the earth; therefore, the exact application of these images depends on the adopted interpretive reading.
